newsitem.title: INDIA: India court clears more accused in corruption case.
newsitem.headline: India court clears more accused in corruption case.

text.p: The government's case in one of India's most notorious corruption scandals unravelled further on Wednesday when a court threw out charges against four former ministers from the Congress party, news agencies said.

They said a Delhi court dismissed money laundering cases against the four Congress party members, saying the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) had presented inadequate evidence to back up the charges.
Special judge V.B. Gupta cleared R.K. Dhawan, Madhavrao Scindia, Arjun Singh and Narayan Dutt Tiwari in the $18 million scandal, the agencies said.
The bribery scandal that broke in January 1996 had forced seven ministers in former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao's government -- including Dhawan and Scindia -- and two governors to resign.
It erupted after a "hawala", or illegal foreign exchange dealer, claimed to have paid more than 100 bureaucrats and politicians bribes in exchange for favours.
The scandal, which also touched some opposition leaders, was widely seen as harming the Congress party, which suffered a humiliating defeat in general elections in April and May of 1996.
Rao stepped down as Congress leader in September after being implicated in three separate corruption cases. He has said he is innocent.

Last month, another Delhi court dropped money laundering cases against the chief of the main opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) party, L.K. Advani, and former Congress minister Vidya Charan Shukla.
The courts dropped the six cases for lack of evidence, saying entries in a diary of alleged money-launderers used by the CBI, India's federal police, to press charges did not suffice as evidence.

Advani resigned his parliamentary seat soon after he was indicted in January 1996, and vowed not to run for office until cleared of the charges. He is now spearheading the BJP's grass-roots campaign to win power in the next poll.
In April a judge also dropped charges against the alleged money launderers, three businessmen brothers called Jain.

The scandal had its roots in the chance arrest of two suspected Kashmiri guerrillas in March 1991 who put police on the track of J.K. Jain, later accused of being a dealer on the illegal foreign exchange market.
Federal investigators said a diary found in the Jain home listed in code the names of 115 politicians and bureaucrats with details of payments that each was alleged to have received.
They said the payments, between April 1988 and March 1991, totalled nearly 655 million rupees ($18.3 million).

The Jain brothers, who run large engineering and fertiliser firms in the northern Indian state of Bihar, were later accused of receiving political favours in return for the payments. ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
